The program

A connected approach
to unmanned flight.

At BANSHEE UAV, students investigate how airframes, controls, power, robotic ground support, and test evidence work together. The program develops these capabilities around shared aircraft and system interfaces rather than as isolated demonstrations.

Platform / SINCHDrone

Vertical flight.
A broader mission.

SINCH provides a common aircraft platform for flight control, structures, aerodynamics, autonomy, manufacturing, and endurance work.

Platform brief

Configuration
VTOL fixed-wing research aircraft
Near-term focus
Controlled hover and configuration understanding
Integration
Autonomy, ground systems, aerodynamics, structures, and energy

Control before transition.

Reliable hover is a foundation for the wider aircraft program. Configuration measurements and controlled tests help separate aerodynamic, structural, propulsion, mass-distribution, and controller effects.

The aircraft is also the integration point for autonomous landing, battery interfaces, solar assistance, and structural changes. Those capabilities are most useful when they can be verified together on a consistent baseline.

Development priority: establish repeatable aircraft behavior before progressing to more complex transition and endurance demonstrations.

Ground systems

The mission continues
after landing.

Robotic ground support explores how an aircraft can align, exchange energy, and prepare for another flight through repeatable mechanical and electrical interfaces.

Robotic Ground Station

The aircraft-ground interface.

The Battery Transfer Pod is a rail-guided robotic mechanism intended to move batteries between the ground-control and battery-storage portions of the system. Current work emphasizes interface baselining, controllable motion, and staged integration.

01 / Alignment

Position the aircraft.

Define landing and mechanical interfaces that place the aircraft predictably for service.

02 / Handling

Move the battery.

Develop the transfer mechanism, mounts, and retention features required for a repeatable exchange.

03 / Integration

Automate the sequence.

Bring motion, sensing, electrical interfaces, and aircraft behavior together through staged testing.

← Back to research

Aerodynamics & experimentation

Understand the flow.
Inform the design.

Aerodynamic work connects analysis, aircraft geometry, and physical testing so configuration changes can be evaluated with evidence.

Analysis connected
to hardware.

Current work includes evaluating wing geometry, testing existing wing hardware, and supporting a SINCH-representative wind-tunnel model. Planned particle image velocimetry (PIV) work will help visualize and quantify flow around the aircraft model.

Aerodynamics works closely with Design & Structures and Manufacturing so analysis can inform buildable changes and experimental models.

Research questions

What changes the aircraft response?

Wing geometry, propulsion placement, mass distribution, and empennage configuration can all change the aircraft's behavior. The team uses simulation and testing to determine which effects matter enough to drive a design change.

Meet the Aerodynamics team↗
← Back to research

Autonomy & avionics

Sense. Decide.
Control.

Flight electronics and software connect pilot commands, autonomous behaviors, telemetry, sensing, and aircraft response.

From bench validation
to flight behavior.

Current avionics work focuses on validating hardware, resolving software issues, and translating autonomy functions into predictable aircraft behavior. The architecture includes a Pixhawk 6C flight controller, an ESP32 microcontroller, radio interfaces, and Mission Planner configuration.

Storm IV remains a useful quadcopter testbed for autonomy and landing behaviors before transferring mature functions to SINCHDrone.

01 / Flight control

Configure the aircraft.

Manage flight-controller parameters and the signals that connect sensors, actuators, and vehicle state.

02 / Autonomy

Develop behaviors.

Advance waypoint, landing, and higher-level logic through staged bench and flight testing.

03 / Telemetry

Use the data.

Compare commanded and observed behavior to identify integration or control issues.

← Back to research

Energy & endurance

More useful energy.
Less integration penalty.

Solar assistance is an aircraft-level trade: useful electrical power must be weighed against mass, wiring, packaging, structure, and aerodynamic effects.

The installation matters.

Energy work is meaningful only when the complete installation is considered. Cell placement, electrical regulation, wiring, added mass, structural attachment, and the effect on aircraft balance all influence the net benefit.

BANSHEE's endurance research therefore connects power work with the wing, avionics, structures, and flight-test plan rather than treating solar hardware as a stand-alone subsystem.

Verification focus

Measure the net effect.

The useful question is not only how much power the solar system can produce, but whether the installed system improves aircraft operation after integration penalties are included.

Development objective: verify useful output and its net effect on the aircraft before making endurance claims.

The program

Student engineering.
System-level thinking.

BANSHEE UAV is a student engineering project at California State Polytechnic University, Pomona. The program connects research with the practical demands of integrated hardware, software, and test.

How the work comes together

Across disciplines.
Around shared interfaces.

Aerodynamics, structures, manufacturing, avionics, robotics, flight testing, and systems engineering work against the same physical aircraft and support architecture.

The design process is iterative: define the problem, build or configure the system, test it, capture what happened, and feed that evidence into the next decision.

Program structure

Specialized work.
Shared verification.

The subteams retain technical ownership of their disciplines while Systems Engineering coordinates interfaces, requirements, risks, and evidence. The result is a program organized around integration rather than isolated deliverables.

Meet the subteams↗

Development / 2026-2027

Progress built
on evidence.

The development sequence prioritizes a serviceable baseline, controlled testing, verified subsystem interfaces, and integration. These are planning priorities rather than claims of completed performance.

01BASELINE

Know the configuration

Record aircraft geometry, mass properties, propulsion hardware, avionics, software settings, and current interfaces.

Intended outcome

A consistent reference configuration for comparison and change control.

02CONTROL

Resolve repeatable hover

Use measured response and controlled tests to investigate instability and evaluate changes across wing, empennage, propulsion, mass distribution, and flight control.

Intended outcome

Repeatable, controlled aircraft behavior with documented evidence.

03INTERFACES

Verify supporting systems

Advance autonomy, ground-system mechanisms, flow research, structural modifications, noise testing, and energy integration through reviewed test stages.

Intended outcome

Evidence that critical subsystem interfaces work as intended.

04INTEGRATE

Progress toward demonstration

Bring mature aircraft and supporting capabilities together without skipping configuration control, test readiness, or verification evidence.

Intended outcome

An integrated demonstration supported by traceable test evidence.

The next step depends
on what the test shows.
